# How scientists can reduce their carbon footprint

## Authors

- Jeremy Nathans<sup>1</sup> †
- Peter Sterling<sup>2</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. Howard Hughes Medical Institute Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine Baltimore United States
2. University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Cutting down on long-distance air travel is the best way to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases by the scientific community.

## The carbon footprint of a scientist

For economy class travel on a commercial airplane, ~1 kg of carbon dioxide is emitted per passenger per 10 kilometers: this means that a flight from the east coast of the United States to central Europe and back (a distance of about 13,000 km) produces 1.3 metric tons of carbon dioxide per passenger. For comparison, a daily round-trip commute of 25 kilometers in a fuel-efficient car produces 1.5 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year. Thus, flying across the Atlantic and back generates roughly the same carbon footprint as a typical year of commuting by car.

To put these numbers in a global perspective, the mean carbon dioxide emission per person per year in the United States is 17 metric tons. Comparable figures for other countries include 9.3 for Japan, 6.7 for China, 5.2 for France, and 1.7 for India (World Bank, 2016). These carbon footprints reflect the total economic activity of a given country, so the carbon dioxide emissions that are under the control of an individual citizen are substantially smaller. Moreover, the per capita carbon footprint is expected to rise substantially in many countries in the developing world over the next 50 years, driven by a broad increase in the standard of living, so citizens in the developed world need to do all they can to start reducing carbon dioxide emissions now.

How does the carbon footprint of air travel compare to the carbon footprint of a typical life sciences laboratory? If we ignore the energy consumed in the heating and cooling of laboratory buildings – values that vary widely depending on locale – we find that most of the carbon footprint is due to refrigerators, freezers and other large items of equipment. For example, it takes ~18 kW-hours per day to operate a freezer at -80°C, which translates into 4 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year (based on the US average of 1.34 pounds of carbon dioxide per kW-hour; Union of Concerned Scientists, 2012). When lighting, cold rooms and smaller items of laboratory equipment (such as computers, spectrophotometers and incubators) are included, we estimate that the equipment in a typical life sciences laboratory of 7–10 people would likely generate more than 20 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year.

It is difficult to envision how life scientists could significantly reduce the carbon footprint associated with operating their laboratories since virtually all of the energy is used to run essential equipment. Thus, long-distance air travel would appear to be the largest source of work-related carbon dioxide emission that the scientific community could easily reduce.

To illustrate the magnitude of the scientific community’s travel-related carbon footprint, consider the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience (SFN), which attracts ~30,000 attendees to the United States from across the globe. By analyzing the cities of origin of attendees at the 2014 SFN meeting in Washington, DC, we estimate the mean round-trip distance traveled per person at ~7,500 kilometers, which gives the meeting a carbon footprint of 22,000 metric tons, roughly equivalent to the annual carbon footprint of 1000 medium-sized laboratories.

## A modest proposal

As a first step in reducing the carbon footprint of the scientific community we propose that all large scientific societies with an annual meeting cut back to one large meeting every two years. To partially compensate, we envision a series of smaller local meetings in alternate years that would bring together hundreds or thousands, rather than tens of thousands, of participants. The proposed change would roughly halve the carbon footprints associated with the largest meetings. We have formally proposed this idea to Dr. Hollis Cline, President of the Society for Neuroscience, and she has agreed to put it before the Society’s council. As a practical matter, any proposed changes in the scheduling of large national or international meetings would likely occur on a time scale of at least 5–10 years because societies have to book convention centers many years in advance. This is all the more reason to start the process sooner rather than later.

We further propose that seminars, grant review panels, interviews and other travel-intensive activities be examined with an eye toward reducing long-distance travel. For each of these activities, we should ask whether there is an equivalent seminar speaker or committee member who could travel 300 km instead of 3,000 km. For activities that do not require a face-to-face meeting, such as grant reviews, we should ask whether remote video-conferencing or a conference call could accomplish the same or nearly the same end. Scientists who do not live and work close to major scientific hubs may fear that a reduction in long-distance travel will lead to scientific isolation. Solutions to this challenge might include traveling with an itinerary that includes multiple clustered destinations and making greater use of electronic communication technology.

We appreciate that face-to-face meetings play an important role in the life of a scientific field. However, the cost-benefit balance has shifted: climate-change costs are long-term and they are going to be staggeringly disruptive. This new reality calls for greater flexibility and greater creativity in how we conduct our business. Fortunately, we are more connected now than ever before, thanks to today’s technology, so we can offset a reduction in face-to-face meetings by making greater use of electronic communication. For example, when one of us (JN) was invited to lecture in Hyderabad, India, the lecture, together with a question-and-answer session, was delivered in real-time via a remote video-link from a studio at Johns Hopkins University in the US. With video screens simultaneously showing the speaker, the audience and the PowerPoint presentation, the experience was remarkably similar to a live presentation. The entire event took the speaker less time than he would have spent driving to the airport and waiting to board the plane to India. It also vacated an airplane seat that would have generated 2.6 metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Reductions in long distance travel by the scientific community, if adopted on a global scale, could reduce carbon dioxide emissions by many hundreds of thousands of metric tons annually. Moreover, a demonstration by the scientific community that it is taking concrete action would be an important step in convincing the general public to consider similar actions. Conversely, if scientists – arguably the most highly educated, informed and intellectually rigorous members of society – do not lead by example, then who else will lead?

In summary, the changes that we propose are not small, but they are modest compared to the changes that will soon be forced upon humanity by anthropogenic climate change.

results.result: A transatlantic flight produces approximately 1.3 metric tons of CO2 per passenger, which is comparable to a year of car commuting (1.5 metric tons). This is based on an emission rate of ~1 kg CO2 per passenger per 10 km for economy class air travel.
results.evaluation: The emission rate (C2) is presented as factual knowledge without citation, and the calculation methodology is not detailed. The comparison depends on assumptions about commuting frequency (daily, presumably ~250 work days) that are not explicitly stated. The car emission estimate (C4) also lacks source documentation. While the arithmetic appears internally consistent, the underlying data sources and assumptions require verification.

results.result: Per capita CO2 emissions vary substantially by country (US: 17, Japan: 9.3, China: 6.7, France: 5.2, India: 1.7 metric tons/year), but individual controllable emissions are substantially smaller than these national averages.
results.evaluation: The national emission data (C6-C10) are properly cited to World Bank 2016, providing verifiable support. The inference (C11) that individual controllable emissions are smaller than total per capita footprints is logically sound, as national figures include industrial, governmental, and infrastructure emissions beyond individual control.

results.result: Per capita carbon footprints in developing countries are expected to rise substantially over the next 50 years due to increasing standards of living, necessitating immediate emission reductions in developed countries.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are presented as predictions without supporting citations or quantitative projections. While the general trend is consistent with development economics, the lack of specific data or modeling makes this speculative. The normative conclusion (C14) follows logically only if the prediction is accurate, but no evidence is provided for the underlying forecast.

results.result: A typical life sciences laboratory of 7-10 people generates more than 20 metric tons of CO2 annually, primarily from equipment like -80°C freezers (4 metric tons/year each), with most energy use being essential and difficult to reduce.
results.evaluation: The freezer energy consumption (C16) and US emission conversion factor (C18) are presented as data, with C18 cited. However, the overall laboratory estimate (C19) is acknowledged as an estimate without detailed methodology. The claim that equipment energy use is essential (C15) lacks supporting analysis of potential efficiency improvements or alternative technologies. No data on measurement methods, sample size, or variability across laboratories is provided.

results.result: Long-distance air travel is identified as the largest easily reducible source of work-related CO2 emissions for scientists, making it the best target for emission reductions by the scientific community.
results.evaluation: This conclusion (C1, C21) relies on the unsubstantiated claim (C20) that laboratory emissions cannot be significantly reduced. No systematic analysis of alternative reduction strategies is presented. The comparison ignores other potential sources (commuting, building operations, computing infrastructure) and does not quantify 'ease' of reduction. The claim that air travel is 'best' requires comparative analysis of cost-effectiveness, feasibility, and impact across all emission sources, which is not provided.

results.result: The 2014 Society for Neuroscience meeting generated approximately 22,000 metric tons of CO2 from 30,000 attendees traveling an average of 7,500 km round-trip, equivalent to the annual emissions of 1,000 medium-sized laboratories.
results.evaluation: While the attendee count (C22) appears factual, the mean travel distance (C23) is based on an undescribed analysis methodology. No information is provided about data sources, sampling methods, or how cities of origin were determined. The calculation (C24) assumes all attendees flew, ignoring local participants who may have driven or used public transit. The comparison to laboratories (C25) depends on the uncertain laboratory emission estimate from C19.

results.result: The authors propose that large scientific societies shift to biennial meetings supplemented by smaller regional meetings, which would roughly halve emissions from major conferences, with implementation requiring 5-10 years. This proposal has been formally submitted to the Society for Neuroscience.
results.evaluation: The claim that biennial meetings would 'roughly halve' emissions (C28) is overly simplistic and ignores several factors: (1) smaller regional meetings (C27) would generate their own emissions, which are not quantified; (2) scientists might attend multiple regional meetings instead of one large meeting; (3) no analysis of whether scientific productivity or collaboration would be maintained. The procedural claims (C29-C30) about the SFN proposal are factual statements, but the 5-10 year timeline (C31) is presented without supporting analysis of booking constraints.

results.result: The authors propose examining seminars, grant reviews, and other activities to reduce travel through video-conferencing and strategic trip planning, while acknowledging concerns about scientific isolation for researchers in remote locations.
results.evaluation: These are proposals (C32, C33, C35) rather than demonstrated results. No evidence is provided that video-conferencing achieves 'the same or nearly the same end' (C33) as in-person meetings for activities like grant reviews. The concern about isolation (C34) is acknowledged but the proposed solutions (C35) are not evaluated for effectiveness. No data on current practices, potential adoption rates, or actual emission reductions are provided.

results.result: While face-to-face meetings are important, the cost-benefit balance has shifted due to severe climate change impacts, and modern communication technology can offset reductions in physical meetings.
results.evaluation: The claim about climate change disruption (C38) reflects scientific consensus but is presented without specific citations. The assertion that technology can 'offset' reduced face-to-face interaction (C40) is speculative and not supported by evidence about effectiveness for scientific collaboration, networking, or career development. No studies are cited comparing outcomes of virtual versus in-person scientific interactions.

results.result: A remote lecture delivered via video-link from Johns Hopkins to Hyderabad, India provided an experience remarkably similar to live presentation while saving time and avoiding 2.6 metric tons of CO2 emissions.
results.evaluation: This is a single anecdotal case (C41-C42) with subjective assessment (C43). The claim that the experience was 'remarkably similar' is not supported by objective measures or audience feedback. The time savings (C44) and emission calculation (C45) are plausible but the generalizability of this single positive experience to all scientific communication is not established. No discussion of technical requirements, costs, or accessibility barriers is provided.

results.result: Global adoption of reduced scientific travel could save hundreds of thousands of metric tons of CO2 annually, and scientists have a responsibility to lead by example given their education and the severity of climate change.
results.evaluation: The quantitative claim (C46) is speculative extrapolation without supporting calculation or data on total scientific travel. The assertion about public influence (C47) is unsupported by evidence from behavioral science or public opinion research. The rhetorical argument about scientific leadership (C48-C49) is normative rather than empirical. The comparison to future climate impacts (C50) lacks specific quantitative analysis of the relative scale of proposed changes versus predicted climate disruption.
